implementation_notes: Moq's partial mock is the .NET spy for class collaborators: new Mock<Mailer> { CallBase = true } invokes the real virtual implementation for members without a setup, and mock.Verify(m => m.Send(...), Times.Once) asserts the recorded interactions after the SUT ran. What replaces the classic spy object is CallBase delegation plus expression-based verification; for interfaces (no base implementation) use NSubstitute's Received()/DidNotReceive() style or a hand-written recorder instead.
pitfalls: CallBase requires the member to be overridable (virtual/abstract); sealed or non-virtual members run nothing and Verify then checks the mock's silent no-op.
Moq matches arguments by reference for reference types unless It.Is/It.IsAny is used, so exactness creeps in - assert the arguments the contract names.
MockBehavior.Strict (default is Loose) changes the failure mode: unexpected calls throw instead of being recorded, erasing the spy's record-everything property.

variants.name: NSubstitute substitutes with Received()/DidNotReceive()
variants.implementation_notes: NSubstitute substitutes record every call: after the SUT runs, command.Received().Execute() asserts at least one call, Received(3) an exact count and DidNotReceive() zero, with Arg.Is/Arg.Any matchers narrowing the assertion to specific arguments. What replaces the classic spy object is the substitute itself - an auto-recording double configured with fluent callbacks instead of expected sequences.
pitfalls: Received() asserts 'at least one call', so a duplicate invocation passes unless Received(n) is used explicitly.
Argument matchers must be used consistently inside Received() calls when precision matters; mixing raw values and Arg.Is can throw and is easy to misread.
Substitutes return default values unless configured, so unconfigured paths may pass through the SUT differently than the real collaborator would.
